title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)
authors: Chinmay Katke, C. Nadir Kaplan
abstract: We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.

infographic.key_insight: Variational functional neural networks (vfNN) find physical states by optimizing continuum functionals directly rather than solving their Euler–Lagrange differential equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a route to physics-based neural solvers using lower-order derivatives and physical scales instead of ad hoc loss weights.
method: Represent system states with a neural network and optimize an integral-form physical functional.
Use lower-order derivatives and physically grounded scales rather than conventional PINN residual losses.
Combine quasi-Newton optimization with simulated annealing to target solutions regardless of their stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate simulations on benchmark systems governed by linear and nonlinear ordinary differential equations, without quantitative error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Nonconvex optimization and unstable stationary solutions complicate convergence; broader performance beyond the reported ODE benchmarks remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
authors: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network with exact boundary and initial constraints accurately recovers the shear piezoelectric coefficient e₁₅ from sparse, noisy simulated wavefields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could enable nondestructive characterization of shear-mode coupling in PMUTs and surface acoustic wave devices without dedicated resonance-test specimens.
method: Embed spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers into network outputs to enforce boundary and initial conditions exactly.
Train on coupled electro-elastodynamic equations and sparse observations, eliminating boundary and initial-condition penalty weights.
Nondimensionalize governing coefficients to comparable scales for optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: On finite-element data sampled along one subsurface line, mean e₁₅ error was 1.19% at 30 dB noise and 0.65–2.71% across a 40–0 dB noise sweep.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to simulated plane-strain PZT-5H data; performance on physical measurements and more complex geometries remains untested.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints

title: Bridging Neural Tangent Kernel Analysis and Reinforcement Learning for Deep Function Approximation
authors: William St-Arnaud, Margarida Carvalho, Golnoosh Farnadi
abstract: Despite their widespread success across machine learning, the learning dynamics and generalization properties of neural networks remain poorly understood. The neural tangent kernel (NTK) provides an analytical characterization of the learning dynamics of infinitely wide neural networks and serves as a useful proxy for finite-width networks in supervised learning. In this work, we extend the NTK framework to reinforcement learning (RL) by introducing a temporal-difference (TD) flow formulation that accommodates time-varying mini-batches and TD targets, yielding a closed-form solution for value function evolution in an overparametrized setting. We also devise an optimization-based state-space exploration method that leverages the closed-form solution, coupled with constraints on the environment, to model the set of feasible states. On a deterministic grid environment, we validate that the proposed RL-based NTK formulation is indeed learning efficiently and adapting to the distribution shift in the training data distribution, and we demonstrate that the resulting exploration strategy improves sample efficiency. To our knowledge, this is the first work to extend NTK theory to characterize the learning dynamics of RL training with time-varying mini-batches and TD updates.

infographic.key_insight: A temporal-difference flow extends neural tangent kernel analysis to RL with time-varying mini-batches and targets, yielding a closed-form description of value-function evolution in an overparameterized setting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation enables optimization-based exploration that incorporates environment constraints and can improve sample efficiency.
method: Formulate NTK-based temporal-difference dynamics with changing mini-batches and targets.
Derive a closed-form solution for value-function evolution.
Use the solution and environment constraints to guide state-space exploration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments in a deterministic grid environment demonstrate adaptation to training-distribution shifts and improved sample efficiency from the exploration strategy.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to a deterministic grid environment; applicability to finite-width networks and more complex or stochastic environments remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Bridging Neural Tangent Kernel Analysis and Reinforcement Learning for Deep Function Approximation

title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
authors: Rileigh Bandy, Teresa Portone, Mohammad Khalil, Eric Crislip, Kyle Neal
abstract: Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

infographic.key_insight: For a synthetic epidemiological model, embedded closure learning achieves the best average accuracy, while staged learning trades moderately higher error for substantially fewer model evaluations and more robust optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Staged closure learning can reduce training costs when repeated simulator calls are expensive and qualitative predictive behavior is sufficient.
method: Compare embedded and staged data-driven closure learning in a synthetic susceptible–infected–quarantined–recovered (SIQR) model.
Use data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations.
Train the staged machine-learning closure offline on assimilated trajectories rather than repeatedly invoking the simulator.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on an SIQR model with a nonlinear, state-dependent quarantine closure shows comparable qualitative behavior for staged learning, but moderately greater error than embedded training.
infographic.watch_item: The reported trade-off is demonstrated on one synthetic model and may not generalize to other dynamical systems.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches

title: Can We Stop the Backtest Yet? Anytime-Valid Promotion Tests for Adaptive Financial Research Agents
authors: Eric Benhamou, Jean-Jacques Ohana, Beatrice Guez, Ethan Setrouk, Chamyl Saadi, Thomas Jacquot
abstract: Financial research agents can generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the resulting selection process. Candidates appear at data-dependent times, weak rules are abandoned, and promising ones are watched until they cross a reporting threshold. We introduce PROMOTE, a protocol that assigns every candidate predictable testing wealth at birth and accumulates a cost-aware e-process only from subsequent returns. If lifetime allocations sum to at most one, a weighted Ville argument bounds the probability of ever promoting a rule whose declared bounded net score has always had nonpositive conditional mean. The result permits dependent candidates, adaptive births, and indefinite monitoring. We audit the implementation in two settings. A retrospective pseudo-out-of-sample replay contains 24 panel--rule hypotheses, 3,000 shared-sign null paths, injected alternatives, and public ETF and industry data. Repeated unadjusted tests produce a family crossing in 94.5% of null paths, versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; at a 15-bp aligned ETF-component perturbation, PROMOTE has 70.1% target power and median crossing session 2,327. A separate exact mean-zero experiment lets an agent select candidate identities and birth times from past scores; the funded gate has 1.77% false-family crossings across 3,000 programs. The market replay produces zero promotions after costs. The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null; it is not a certificate that an earlier edge remains profitable at deployment. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.

infographic.key_insight: PROMOTE bounds the probability of ever falsely promoting a trading rule despite adaptive candidate creation, dependent tests, and indefinite monitoring.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Financial research agents can use PROMOTE as a cost-aware statistical gate before promoting strategies discovered through continuous experimentation.
method: Assign each candidate predictable testing wealth at birth, with lifetime allocations totaling at most one.
Accumulate a cost-aware e-process using only post-birth returns.
Apply a weighted Ville bound to control false promotion under the declared bounded-score null.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 3,000 shared-sign null paths testing 24 hypotheses, false-family crossings were 94.5% for repeated unadjusted tests versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; a separate adaptive mean-zero experiment recorded 1.77% across 3,000 programs.
infographic.watch_item: The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null, not future profitability; the market replay produced no promotions after costs.
infographic.paper_title: Can We Stop the Backtest Yet? Anytime-Valid Promotion Tests for Adaptive Financial Research Agents

title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization
authors: Gabriele Oliaro, Jaeseong Lee, Zhaoyuan Su, Sreeram Vennam, Zhihao Jia, Samyam Rajbhandari
abstract: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.46x FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean). Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.

infographic.key_insight: KernelSeek steers GPU kernel optimization with timely questions rather than more tools or fixed recipes, helping a general-purpose coding agent challenge bottlenecks and explore new optimization paths.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Question-driven guidance could help engineers optimize CUDA kernels without operator-specific agent knowledge or a faster implementation to imitate.
method: Pair a general-purpose coding agent with a minimal harness enforcing a verifiable optimization goal.
Ask questions at decision points, initially from a human and later from a self-applied question bank.
Redirect attention across system layers and challenge claimed performance limits without prescribing implementations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The reported dependency-free attention forward kernels passed all 182 scenarios per architecture and achieved geometric-mean speedups of 1.16× over FlashAttention-3 on Hopper and 1.46× over FlashAttention-4 on Blackwell.
infographic.watch_item: The workflow initially relied on human questions, and the abstract does not establish how well fully autonomous questioning generalizes beyond attention kernels.
infographic.paper_title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization

title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
authors: Tom Saliencro, Wen-Hsuan Liu, Rohan Desai, Amara Okonkwo, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

infographic.key_insight: BISECT addresses spectral starvation in continual LoRA learning by splitting a fixed low-rank budget between shared feature directions and task-specific novelty instead of enforcing strict historical-subspace isolation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It supports exemplar-free continual adaptation of pretrained Vision Transformers while merging updates into the backbone with no extra inference parameters or FLOPs.
method: Build an invariant carrier from dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix.
Extract an orthogonal novelty complement using generalized Rayleigh whitening and complement projection.
Merge trained updates using current-to-joint Rayleigh ratios to gate invariant atoms, while retaining novelty atoms at unit gain.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that historical null tails capture only 5.5% of incoming-task variance and that BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines across eight incremental settings on five image datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Training-time costs and numerical stability of Gram-matrix decomposition and whitening need assessment; zero added inference cost does not establish low adaptation overhead.
infographic.paper_title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning

title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
authors: Wen-Hsuan Liu, Amara Okonkwo, Tom Saliencro, Rohan Desai, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.

infographic.key_insight: RASP separates reading from writing: inference uses every LoRA atom, while training updates only a sparse subset within a single fixed-size adapter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This design keeps adapter parameter storage constant across sequential vision tasks without reducing the available LoRA rank at inference.
method: A scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-q unlocked atoms for gradient updates while inference reads all atoms.
A Frobenius Gram coherence penalty separates active output directions from non-updated directions.
Router activation history and atom spectral norms determine a consolidation index for Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports matching or surpassing branch-expanding LoRA learners on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A under a constant adapter parameter footprint, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Long-horizon learning may depend on how sparsity and anchor locking preserve enough unlocked capacity; the abstract does not quantify this trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA

title: A Physics Informed Neural Network Approach to Decipher Environmental Confinement of Molecular Clouds in the Third Galactic Quadrant
authors: Ashok Mondal
abstract: Recent high-sensitivity and high-resolution surveys of the Third Galactic Quadrant [$219.75 \leq l \leq 229.75$ and $-5.25 \leq b \leq 5.25$], such as the Milky Way Imaging Scroll Painting ( MWISP) survey, have revealed a significant population of molecular clouds (MCs) that appear virially unbound ($α_{vir} > 2$) according to traditional isolated MC models. However, these apparently unstable cloud structures are actually found long-lived and actively undertaking star formation. This inconsistency presents a Virial Paradox. In the present work, we employ a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) to address this discrepancy by re-evaluating the stability of 2,091 MCs . Unlike traditional machine learning, our PINN model embeds the complete Eulerian Virial Theorem including external surface pressure support ($P_{ext}$) directly into the network's loss function. This model autonomously discovers a global Galactic pressure field that scales inversely with vertical height ($|z|$) and Galactocentric radius ($R_{GC}$), consistent with the properties of the Galactic Flare. By incorporating this AI-derived pressure support, we demonstrate a dramatic shift in the stability census: 99.9\% of previously thought unbound clouds are found to be in a state of pressure confined equilibrium ($α_{AI} \leq 2$). Furthermore, we find a robust log-log correlation ($R = 0.64$) between our corrected stability parameter and the star formation rate (SFR). This correlation provides independent physical validation that environmental confinement is a primary regulator of star forming efficiency in the outer Galaxy.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network infers external pressure that places 99.9% of previously classified unbound molecular clouds into pressure-confined equilibrium.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Embedding physical balance laws in neural-network losses can help infer environmental effects missing from isolated-system models.
method: Reassess 2,091 molecular clouds in the Third Galactic Quadrant using a physics-informed neural network.
Embed the complete Eulerian Virial Theorem, including external surface pressure, in the loss function.
Infer a Galactic pressure field that decreases with vertical height and Galactocentric radius.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 99.9% reclassification of previously unbound clouds and a log-log correlation of R = 0.64 between corrected stability and star formation rate.
infographic.watch_item: The inferred pressure field needs independent observational validation; the reported correlation alone does not establish causal regulation of star formation.
infographic.paper_title: A Physics Informed Neural Network Approach to Decipher Environmental Confinement of Molecular Clouds in the Third Galactic Quadrant

title: Optimize the Harness, Not the Model: Fitting a Minimal Agent to a Self-Hostable LLM for Investigative Analysis
authors: Shai Nahum Gefen, Vered Chassida, Dmitry Basin, Guy Feigenblat
abstract: Government intelligence teams need LLM agents that can analyze large, messy evidence collections, but security and cost constraints often rule out hosted frontier models and broad, hard-to-audit tool surfaces. We report CLEO: Constrained Loop for Environment Optimization, a method for fitting a minimal agent harness to a fixed, self-hostable LLM. Given an expert-validated dataset, CLEO admits only the tools, guardrails, memory policies, and loop components that improve accuracy while remaining general and auditable. On our held-out dataset, the CLEO harness reaches an 83.8% pass rate, within 1.2 points of the strongest out-of-the-box Claude Code SDK baseline, while being two orders of magnitude smaller.

infographic.key_insight: CLEO fits a minimal, auditable agent harness to a fixed self-hostable LLM, achieving 83.8% held-out pass rate within 1.2 percentage points of the strongest out-of-the-box Claude Code SDK baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing the harness rather than the model offers a path toward investigative agents under security, cost, and auditability constraints.
method: Keep the self-hostable LLM fixed and optimize its surrounding agent harness.
Use expert-validated data to admit only accuracy-improving tools, guardrails, memory policies, and loop components.
Require admitted components to remain general and auditable.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an 83.8% pass rate on a held-out dataset with a harness two orders of magnitude smaller, but does not specify dataset size or the harness-size metric.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the reported investigative dataset remains unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Optimize the Harness, Not the Model: Fitting a Minimal Agent to a Self-Hostable LLM for Investigative Analysis

title: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR
authors: Ziqi Pang, Yu-Xiong Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies. We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x for equations f(x)=y, where f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g., more solutions, longer y, etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking, since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking.

infographic.key_insight: RLVR can teach accurate step-by-step reasoning in-distribution yet fail under harder shifts by reverting to ineffective brute-force enumeration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Training-task design can influence whether outcome-rewarded models retain effective reasoning strategies beyond their training distribution.
method: Use non-bijective string equations f(x)=y requiring multiple input solutions.
Test easy-to-hard shifts, including more solutions and longer outputs.
Co-train with bijective inversion tasks to reinforce derivation without process supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the controlled equation-solving framework, OOD shifts caused sharp accuracy drops and strategy collapse, while bijective co-training substantially restored derivation and accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a controlled string-equation setting; transfer to broader reasoning tasks remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR

title: Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users Across Skill Levels
authors: Difan Jiao, George Eilender, Zhenwei Tang, Ashton Anderson
abstract: Generative models increasingly simulate users at different skill levels in education and AI evaluation. Yet it remains unclear whether lower-skill behavior reflects less internal knowledge or a different use of retained knowledge. This distinction is difficult to study in natural language, where proficiency and relevant knowledge are hard to measure. In this work, we study Maia-2, a chess transformer that predicts human moves conditioned on player skill, using quantitative skill ratings and deterministically labeled chess concepts. We hold board positions and model weights fixed and analyze positions where skill conditioning changes the prediction from a blunder to the best move. First, we measure encoded knowledge by training probes to predict the presence of 172 chess concepts from Maia-2's internal states. Probe accuracy remains nearly constant across skill conditions, and probes trained at one level transfer accurately to the others. To test whether stronger decisions can be recovered from this retained knowledge, we fine-tune only Maia-2's final output layer, raising best-move accuracy in the lowest skill band from 14.4% to 82.8%. Training this layer only on highest-skill representations retains most of the improvement at lower levels, showing that recovery does not require direct training on lower-skill states. Steering concept-relevant features learned by a sparse autoencoder also improves lower-skill decisions while leaving probe-measured concept encoding practically unchanged. These results support an account in which skill conditioning changes how retained concept knowledge influences move selection, showing that weaker behavior can understate the knowledge available within a model.

infographic.key_insight: Maia-2’s weaker chess play under low-skill conditioning reflects altered use of retained knowledge rather than a measurable loss of concept knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: When building skill-conditioned simulators, evaluate internal knowledge separately from output quality because weak behavior can mask stronger available capabilities.
method: Hold board positions and model weights fixed; analyze cases where skill conditioning switches predictions from blunders to best moves.
Probe internal states for 172 chess concepts and test probe transfer across skill levels.
Test knowledge recovery through output-layer-only fine-tuning and sparse-autoencoder feature steering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Concept-probe accuracy stayed nearly constant across skill conditions, while output-layer fine-tuning raised lowest-skill best-move accuracy from 14.4% to 82.8% on the studied positions.
infographic.watch_item: Findings concern selected skill-sensitive chess positions; generalization to broader gameplay or natural-language user simulation remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users Across Skill Levels

title: Certifying Graph Neural Networks Against Label and Structure Poisoning
authors: Lukas Gosch, Xichuan Chen, Yan Scholten, Stephan Günnemann
abstract: Robust machine learning for graph-structured data has made significant progress against test-time attacks, yet certified robustness to poisoning - where adversaries manipulate the training data - remains largely underexplored. For image data, state-of-the-art poisoning certificates rely on partitioning-and-aggregation schemes. However, we show that these methods fail when applied in the graph domain due to the inherent label and structure sparsity found in common graph datasets, making effective graph-partitioning difficult. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework called deep Self-Training Graph Partition Aggregation (ST-GPA), which enriches each graph partition with informative pseudo-labels and synthetic edges, enabling effective certification against node-label and graph-structure poisoning under sparse conditions. Our method is architecture-agnostic, scales to large numbers of partitions, and consistently and significantly improves robustness guarantees against both label and structure poisoning across multiple benchmarks, while maintaining strong clean accuracy. Overall, our results establish a promising direction for certifiably robust learning on graph-structured data against poisoning under sparse conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Deep Self-Training Graph Partition Aggregation (ST-GPA) strengthens certified robustness to training-time label and graph-structure poisoning by addressing sparsity within graph partitions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture-agnostic framework offers a way to add poisoning robustness guarantees to graph-learning pipelines while maintaining strong clean accuracy.
method: Partition graph data for partition-and-aggregation certification.
Enrich sparse partitions with informative pseudo-labels and synthetic edges through deep self-training.
Aggregate partition-level predictions to certify robustness against label and structure poisoning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple benchmarks, the abstract reports consistently and significantly improved robustness guarantees against both poisoning types, strong clean accuracy, and scalability to large numbers of partitions.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify certified attack budgets or computational overhead, so deployment-specific robustness and cost require further assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Certifying Graph Neural Networks Against Label and Structure Poisoning

title: Structured Visual Landscape: Generating Preferred Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks
authors: Yusong Zhao, Edgar Y. Walker, Hao Wang, Mi Lu
abstract: Understanding how neurons respond to visual stimulus is an important question in both deep learning and neuroscience. It has significant implications for enhancing the interpretability of black-box artificial neural networks and for understanding the visual representation in the human brain. We propose a structured visual representations landscape and design an activation-based prior that allows us to effectively regularize the landscape with activations from brain regions or neural network units. Our model Vis-Lens integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model into an image generation framework. It enables the generation of natural, realistic preferred images by directly modifying the activation-regularized latent codes without per-image iterative optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on both artificial neural networks and human visual cortex using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Our framework improves activation modulation and image realism compared with a recent state-of-the-art method for generating preferred visual representations of these neural targets.

infographic.key_insight: Vis-Lens generates natural-looking images preferred by neural targets by directly modifying activation-regularized latent codes, without per-image iterative optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports neural-network interpretability by generating realistic images that reveal the visual patterns favored by selected units.
method: Structure a visual representation landscape using an activation-based prior.
Integrate a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model for image generation.
Modify activation-regularized latent codes to target brain regions or artificial neural units.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on artificial neural networks and human visual cortex using fMRI data report improved activation modulation and image realism over a recent state-of-the-art method.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative gains or computational costs, leaving the practical size of the improvement unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Structured Visual Landscape: Generating Preferred Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks

title: Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning
authors: Atsutomo Yara, Yoshikazu Terada
abstract: We consider nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation of the intensity function of a Poisson process, allowing the intensity to depend on observed covariates. Such models describe how event rates vary with external conditions, including conditions under which the intensity becomes arbitrarily small or vanishes. However, risk analysis based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence typically requires the true intensity to be bounded away from zero, a restrictive assumption in applications. We develop a unified approach that avoids this assumption and derive an oracle inequality for the covariate-averaged Hellinger distance between the true intensity and the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE). As an application of the oracle inequality, we establish convergence rates for NPMLEs based on deep neural networks (DNNs). Our results show that, as in nonparametric regression, the ability of DNNs to capture underlying structure leads to improved convergence rates. Specifically, DNN-based NPMLEs mitigate the curse of dimensionality when the true intensity has a compositional structure and automatically adapt to a low-dimensional Riemannian manifold structure of the event space. For intensity functions with a compositional structure, DNN-based NPMLEs achieve nearly minimax-optimal convergence rates without explicitly incorporating this structure into the network architecture. Simulations demonstrate that DNN-based estimators outperform kernel estimators in most settings, while manifold kernels remain competitive in some designs. Finally, we analyze stimulus-evoked neural spiking using data from the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels project. DNN-based NPMLEs provide better out-of-sample performance than a conditional kernel estimator, as evaluated by held-out log-likelihood.

infographic.key_insight: Deep neural network intensity estimators achieve structure-adaptive convergence guarantees for covariate-driven Poisson processes, even when the true intensity can vanish.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports flexible event-rate modeling under changing external conditions while reducing dimensionality burdens when compositional or manifold structure is present.
method: Estimate covariate-dependent intensity by nonparametric maximum likelihood.
Derive an oracle inequality using covariate-averaged Hellinger distance without a positive lower bound on intensity.
Use DNN estimators to exploit compositional structure and adapt to low-dimensional event-space manifolds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations favor DNN estimators over kernels in most settings, and Allen Brain Observatory neural-spiking data show better held-out log-likelihood than a conditional kernel estimator.
infographic.watch_item: Performance gains are not universal: manifold kernels remain competitive in some simulation designs.
infographic.paper_title: Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning

title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics
authors: Meenu Krishnan U., Maryam Hakimzadeh, Indrashish Saha, Meer Mehran Rashid, Lori Graham-Brady, Somdatta Goswami
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly proposed to replace phase-field fracture simulations in many-query tasks such as uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design. Little controlled evidence shows which architectures are reliable, for which fracture problems and how far beyond their training data. We introduce Fracture-Bench, an open benchmark of two phase-field datasets with fixed splits, common test metrics and a description of each dataset's physical regime. Dataset~1 contains 1,000 AT2 simulations of multiple cracks growing from a notched hole in a hyperelastic plate under random non-uniform biaxial boundary displacements (44 load steps, $128\times128$ grid). Dataset~2 contains 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with two inclusions, each ten times stiffer or more compliant than the matrix ($128\times256$ grid). We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO), DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, a UNet and a conditional diffusion model on identical splits and compare one test metric per dataset, training time, inference time and model size. On Dataset~1, FNO and Latent DeepONet attain mean test errors of order $10^{-6}$, about ten times lower than UNet and DeepONet. On Dataset~2, the diffusion model is most accurate, with about one sixth of the UNet error, but requires \SI{706}{s} per prediction versus \SI{6}{ms} for UNet. For all architectures, most of the error occurs in the final load steps, after crack localization. Dataset~2 contains initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths. Architecture rankings therefore depend on the task, and errors averaged over densely sampled inputs reveal little about near-bifurcation cases. Data, codes, splits, regime descriptors and generalization splits are public, with a protocol for adding under-represented regimes such as mixed-mode, three-dimensional and experimentally paired fracture.

infographic.key_insight: No surrogate wins universally: FNO and Latent DeepONet lead on one fracture dataset, while diffusion is most accurate but far slower on the other.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fracture-Bench helps engineers compare surrogate accuracy and computational cost before using them for uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis or design.
method: Benchmark two phase-field regimes: 1,000 AT2 simulations and 4,000 PF-CZM simulations.
Compare FNO, DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, UNet and conditional diffusion using identical splits.
Report dataset-specific test error, training time, inference time and model size.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Dataset 1, FNO and Latent DeepONet achieve mean errors of order 10⁻⁶; on Dataset 2, diffusion has about one-sixth the UNet error but takes 706 s per prediction versus 6 ms.
infographic.watch_item: Average errors can obscure near-bifurcation failures: initial cracks less than one grid cell apart can produce qualitatively different paths, and errors concentrate after crack localization.
infographic.paper_title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics

title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation
authors: Mohammad Pedramfar, Rajiv Khanna, Christopher John Quinn, Vaneet Aggarwal
abstract: Convexity has three equivalent descriptions: support by affine functions, monotonicity of the subdifferential, and increasing secant slopes. We weaken all three by one distortion with parameter $γ\in(0,1]$, which multiplies positive changes by $γ$ and divides negative ones by $γ$. The resulting classes are the convex functions at $γ=1$ and, for $γ<1$, are distinct and nested, with the parameter dropping by at most a square along the chain. For proper lower semicontinuous functions in these classes, the effective domain is convex, local minimizers are global, and the function is locally Lipschitz on the relative interior of its domain. The classes separate offline from online optimization over compact convex sets with efficient projection, with access to function values and bounded support vectors. A smooth member of any class can be minimized to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$ with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ first-order queries and projections. Online, with nonpositive losses and $α$-regret measured against $α$ times the best fixed point, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves $γ$-regret $O(\sqrt T)$ on the largest class. For every fixed, effectively specified $γ\in(0,1)$ and every $α\in(γ,1]$, no randomized polynomial-time algorithm has sublinear expected $α$-regret unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, already for smooth concave polynomial losses in the smallest class, each minimized by one linear optimization. Thus, unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, $γ$ is the exact online coefficient of each class, while the offline coefficient is one.

infographic.key_insight: Tilted convexity preserves arbitrarily accurate offline minimization but has an exact online coefficient of γ, unless NP = RP.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For objectives satisfying these conditions, efficient offline optimization does not imply equally strong guarantees for sequential decision-making.
method: Apply a γ-dependent distortion to affine support, subdifferential monotonicity, and increasing secant slopes.
Establish three nested function classes with convex domains and no nonglobal local minima.
Prove offline approximation guarantees, online γ-regret bounds, and matching computational hardness.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results rather than empirical evaluation: polynomial-query offline ε-accuracy for smooth members and polynomial-time O(√T) online γ-regret on the largest class.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees require the stated oracle and projection access; the online result assumes nonpositive losses, and hardness for coefficients above γ is conditional on NP ≠ RP.
infographic.paper_title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation

title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?
authors: Shanshan Zhong, Chen Xu, Jingjie Ning, Zhengzhong Liu, Aviral Kumar, Chenyan Xiong
abstract: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026. Our experiments span six contemporary language models and four research areas from established to emerging fields, covering more than 90{,}000 proposals in total. LLM agents fall well short of human communities in both the literature they cite and the ideas they state, reaching about 26\% of the human level on citation matching and only 18\% on idea matching. Their populations can cite as diversely as a community and take up its tasks and methods, yet rarely arrive at the concrete approaches and research plans it pursues. Neither richer field context nor larger populations substantially close this gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success, echoing their gap in concrete approaches, and those whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst, suggesting weaker directions rather than overlooked opportunities. These results indicate that the main bottleneck in AI research taste lies less in finding the directions a community works on than in turning them into the concrete approaches it goes on to pursue. We release IdeaTaste as an open, continuously updated leaderboard (https://cxcscmu.github.io/IdeaTaste) that benchmarks contemporary AI proposals against future publication cycles.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs identify research directions but struggle to turn them into concrete approaches pursued by human research communities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI research agents need stronger evaluation of concrete methods and research plans, not just literature coverage or proposal presentation.
method: Generate proposals from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025.
Compare citations and ideas with papers published by the same communities in 2026.
Use blinded expert review to assess proposal quality.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six language models, four research areas, and over 90,000 proposals, LLMs reached about 26% of the human citation-matching level and 18% of the human idea-matching level.
infographic.watch_item: Matching future publications measures alignment with community choices, not whether unmatched ideas could ultimately prove valuable.
infographic.paper_title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?

title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?
authors: Kara D. Lamb
abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents can help develop Earth system parameterizations, but retuned physical schemes remained strong, computationally cheaper alternatives to many learned closures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent-generated differentiable JAX code could accelerate parameterization prototyping, provided physical constraints and simulation performance are validated.
method: Use warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case.
Have agents synthesize literature, reimplement published schemes, and propose new closures.
Compare conventional, learned, and agent-generated parameterizations against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across ten language models, iterative feedback reduced median rollout error for eight; two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures slightly beat the best retuned scheme on held-out rain-mass error.
infographic.watch_item: Unattended performance varied strongly by scheme and language model, and success on this test case does not establish readiness for full Earth system integration.
infographic.paper_title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?

title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
authors: Paulius Skaisgiris, Thomas Pammer, Veronika Semmelrock, Mykyta Ielanskyi, Maximilian Heisinger, Erich Kobler
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.

infographic.key_insight: Pairing LLM-based interpretation with deterministic exact cover solving improves Zebra-puzzle reasoning beyond purely neural approaches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework separates natural-language parsing from symbolic solving, enabling reliable reasoning when the generated formal encoding is correct.
method: An LLM translates puzzle entities and constraints into structured tool calls.
The tool calls construct an exact cover instance for a symbolic solver.
Solver feedback guides iterative repairs of invalid or under- or overconstrained encodings, using expected solution uniqueness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple model scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families, the abstract reports consistent gains over strong neural baselines, including CoT, and recent neuro-symbolic methods.
infographic.watch_item: Solver guarantees apply to the encoded problem; a unique solution alone does not establish faithful translation of the original clues.
infographic.paper_title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
